title: Why farming began when it did
summary: Agriculture began in the Fertile Crescent from about 10,000 BCE, early in the Holocene after the last Ice Age. Several theories, not mutually exclusive, compete to explain why.
why: Farming led to towns, writing and states; its trigger is the hinge of human history.

notes.problem: Source does not mention the Younger Dryas or rising temperatures; demographic theory should carry its proponents.

question: Why did people start farming at the end of the Ice Age, and not earlier?
evidence: Start dated 10,000–8000 BCE in the Fertile Crescent, after the Holocene began 11,700 years ago; the oasis theory now has little support.
wouldSettle: Fine-grained records from early sites linking climate, population and feasting to the first domesticated crops.

theories.name: Hilly Flanks (Braidwood)
theories.idea: Farming began in the Taurus and Zagros hills, where wild ancestors of crops and herds lived.

theories.name: Feasting (Hayden)
theories.idea: Competitive feasts to display power required large food surpluses.

theories.name: Demographic pressure (Sauer, Binford, Flannery)
theories.idea: Growing settled groups outstripped what foraging could supply.

theories.name: Co-evolution (Rindos)
theories.idea: Plants and people co-evolved, from protecting wild plants to full domestication.
